newsitem.title: USA: Study says drinking drivers commonplace in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Study says drinking drivers commonplace in U.S.

text.p: Alcohol-impaired drivers, many of them under age, may hit the road as often as 123 million times a year in the United States, according to a study published on Tuesday.

Alaska, Nevada, Wisconsin, Michigan and North Dakota may have the worst drinking and driving problems, the report from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said. The finding was based on a 1993 telephone survey of 102,263 people age 18 and up.

Those who said they drank were asked how many times in the previous month they had driven after having "perhaps too much to drink?" About 2.5 percent of those surveyed said they had done so at least once.

The report estimated that there were nearly 123 million incidents of alcohol-impaired driving by adults in 1993 -- 101 million among men and 22 million among women -- and that nearly 10 million of those involved 18- to 20-year-olds. The national legal drinking age was 21 when the survey was taken.

"This estimate is 82 times higher than the 1.5 million arrests for driving while intoxicated in the United States that year," the report published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association said.
The estimates were probably conservative, the authors said, because people are reluctant to report that they drink and drive and problem drinkers often deny that they may be impaired.

The estimates per 1,000 population found that the five states with the highest incidence of reported impaired driving were Alaska (1,550), Nevada (1,459), Wisconsin (1,275), Michigan (1,074) and North Dakota (1,009). The national average per 1,000 population was 655.
Maine (165) had the lowest estimate. The survey covered all states except Wyoming as well as the District of Columbia.
